passage: In the staff room after the last bell, Trisha set her pile of Class 7 notebooks down next to Ojas. "Guess who wrote that the Mughals invented cricket?" she said, grinning. Ojas, marking, said, "Hmm." She tried again. "Want to get chaat on the way home?" "Maybe. Let me finish this." She squeezed his shoulder on her way to the kettle. He shifted, pen still moving. Each small miss stung, like stubbing a toe. By the time the kettle clicked, the sting had changed into something harder. "You know, you could look up once in a while," she said, sharper than she meant. Ojas looked up then, startled. "What did I do?"

qa.q: What did Trisha suggest for the way home?
qa.a: She suggested getting chaat on the way home.

qa.q: How did each missed bid feel to Trisha?
qa.a: Each small miss stung, like stubbing a toe, and after enough of them the sting hardened into irritation. 😔

qa.q: What could Ojas do to catch these small bids?
qa.a: He could pause the marking for a moment, laugh at the joke, or say "Chaat sounds good, give me ten minutes", which answers the bid.

qa.q: How does Ojas experience the sharp remark?
qa.a: He is startled and confused, asking "What did I do?", because he did not notice the earlier bids at all.

grounding: Shows a young woman offering small bids for connection, feeling each miss sting, until her requests turn into a complaint.

passage:
Hi Ira,
Remember you asked how being Neil's wife is going? Honestly, it's small things. Yesterday at lunch I sent Neil a meme about our landlord's parrot. Seen, no reply. In the evening I asked about his big presentation. "Fine." I rubbed his shoulders while he was on the laptop and he said "one sec" and never came back from that second. None of it is huge. But each time there's a little sting. I tell myself it's nothing. Then on Saturday I heard myself say, "You never have time for me," and he looked at me like I'd thrown a plate. I didn't mean to complain. I think I was just tired of asking quietly.
Love, Aadhya

qa.q: What did Aadhya send Neil at lunch?
qa.a: She sent Neil a meme about their landlord's parrot.

qa.q: What does Aadhya feel each time a bid is missed?
qa.a: She feels a little sting each time, which she tries to brush off as nothing.

qa.q: What could Aadhya say instead of "You never have time for me"?
qa.a: She could name one clear bid, like "I'd love ten minutes with you tonight, just us", which invites rather than complains.

qa.q: How might Neil have heard "You never have time for me" on Saturday?
qa.a: He probably heard it as an attack out of nowhere, since he hadn't noticed the small missed moments building up.

grounding: Shows a wife making small bids for her husband's attention, feeling each miss sting, until the quiet requests become a complaint.

passage:
Hafsa tried everything that evening in their Kolkata flat.
First a joke: "Your boss called, he says you're fired for being too handsome." Tanvir, on his laptop, said, "Hmm."
Then a question: "Want to see the photos from Rumi's wedding?" "Later."
Then her hand on his shoulder as she passed his chair. He didn't look up.
Each time, a tiny sting. She told herself it was nothing.
By ten, when he finally closed the laptop and said, "What's for dinner?", the sting came out sharp: "Oh, now you notice I exist?"
Tanvir looked startled. From where he sat, it had come out of nowhere.

qa.q: What did Hafsa ask Tanvir about the photos?
qa.a: She asked if he wanted to see the photos from Rumi's wedding.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling each time Tanvir missed her bid?
qa.a: She felt a small sting of hurt, telling herself it was nothing, until it built up into sharpness.

qa.q: What turning point was available before the sharp comment at ten?
qa.a: Hafsa could have said plainly, "I'd love ten minutes with you," or Tanvir could have looked up from the laptop for one of her small bids.

qa.q: What is Tanvir experiencing when Hafsa snaps?
qa.a: He feels startled and confused, because from his side the comment came out of nowhere.

grounding: A young woman offers small bids for attention, a joke, a question, a touch; each missed bid stings, and eventually the request turns into a complaint.

"Look, a pigeon's built a nest on our AC," Heena said, standing at the window.
"Mm," said Vishal, eyes on his phone.
"Should we name it?"
"Sure."
"Vishal Junior?"
No answer.
She sat next to him and leaned her shoulder on his. He shifted slightly to read better.
Heena got up. She came back five minutes later with tea. "Want to go for a walk after this?"
"Tired, yaar."
She put his tea down harder than she needed to. "You're always tired. You're always on that phone. When was the last time you actually talked to me?"
Vishal looked up at last. "Where's this coming from?"

qa.q: What had built a nest on the AC?
qa.a: A pigeon had built a nest on their AC.

qa.q: What was Heena feeling as her small bids kept being missed?
qa.a: She felt hurt and more and more stung, until it came out as frustration and complaint.

qa.q: What turning point was available during this scene?
qa.a: Vishal could have turned toward one of Heena's bids, like naming the pigeon or leaning back, or Heena could have said directly that she missed him before it became a complaint.

qa.q: What is Vishal experiencing when Heena finally complains?
qa.a: He is surprised and confused, not having noticed the string of small bids that came before.

grounding: A young woman makes small bids for attention with jokes, questions and closeness; after enough missed bids, her requests turn into complaints.

passage:
I can almost count the moments, looking back on that month in Kochi.
Monday I sent Thomas a silly photo of a cat on a scooter. Seen, no reply. Small sting.
Tuesday I asked, "Do you want to try the new appam place on Saturday?" He said, "Let's see." Another sting.
Wednesday I rubbed his shoulders while he was on a call. He moved away to hear better.
By Friday, I wasn't asking any more. I was accusing. "You never make time for me. I'm like a flatmate to you."
Thomas was hurt. I was hurt. I'm Anita, and I wish I'd said "I miss you" on Tuesday, instead of "you never" on Friday.

qa.q: What did Anita send Thomas on Monday?
qa.a: A silly photo of a cat on a scooter.

qa.q: What was Anita feeling each time a bid was missed?
qa.a: Anita felt a small sting of hurt each time, and by Friday that hurt had turned into anger and accusation.

qa.q: What turning point was available earlier in the week?
qa.a: On Tuesday Anita could have said plainly that she missed Thomas, before the missed bids built up into "you never" complaints.

qa.q: What was Thomas experiencing when Anita accused him on Friday?
qa.a: He felt hurt and surprised by the accusation, likely not realising how many small bids he had missed.

grounding: A young adult recalls a week of small bids for attention being missed, until the stings turned requests into complaints.

passage:
Couples counselling, session note, week 2.

Indu and Pankaj, married eighteen months. Indu described the past month in detail, and it was clear she has been reaching out many times a day in small ways.

Examples she gave: sending Pankaj a funny video at work, asking about his cricket team, resting her hand on his shoulder while he cooked. Most went unanswered. He admits he often didn't notice.

Indu said each missed moment "stings a little, like a paper cut." After a few weeks, she said, she stopped joking and started saying, "You never listen to me." She was surprised to hear herself.

Pankaj looked genuinely startled to learn the videos had meant anything.

Plan agreed: for one week, each will notice and respond to one small reach from the other per day. We will review next Tuesday.

qa.q: How long have Indu and Pankaj been married?
qa.a: They have been married eighteen months.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when her small reaches were missed?
qa.a: Indu felt a small sting each time, like a paper cut, and over weeks her hurt turned into complaints.

qa.q: Why is the plan to answer one small reach a day a wise step?
qa.a: It makes the small bids visible and gives Indu some response, before her frustration grows into bigger complaints.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel learning that the videos mattered to Indu?
qa.a: Pankaj seems startled and perhaps a little guilty, realising he missed something important without meaning to.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a partner making small bids for attention, feeling stung when they are missed, until requests become complaints.
